flashcards.front: Name the four layers of the TCP/IP model.
flashcards.back_definition: Application (HTTP, DNS), transport (TCP, UDP and ports), internet (IP addresses and routing), and network access (Ethernet, Wi-Fi and MAC addresses).
flashcards.back_example: A web request: HTTP data inside a TCP segment inside an IP packet inside an Ethernet frame.
flashcards.back_confusion: The OSI model has seven layers; TCP/IP folds them into four.
flashcards.back_hook: All Teachers Inspire Networks: application, transport, internet, network access.

flashcards.front: IP address vs MAC address vs port?
flashcards.back_definition: An IP address (32-bit IPv4, 128-bit IPv6) identifies a host across networks. A MAC address (48-bit) identifies a network card on the local segment. A port (16-bit) identifies the service on the host.
flashcards.back_confusion: None of these prove identity: IP and MAC addresses can both be spoofed.
flashcards.back_hook: Street address, front door, flat number.

flashcards.front: What is the TCP three-way handshake?
flashcards.back_definition: SYN from the client, SYN-ACK from the server, ACK from the client; after that the connection is open.
flashcards.back_example: A SYN flood sends many SYNs and never the final ACK, filling the server's half-open connection table.
flashcards.back_confusion: UDP has no handshake, which makes its source addresses easy to spoof.
flashcards.back_hook: Hi? Hi, I hear you. Great, let's talk.

flashcards.back_definition: Forging the source IP address in a packet to hide the sender or impersonate another host.
flashcards.back_example: A reflection DDoS sends small DNS queries with the victim's IP as the source, so large replies hit the victim.
flashcards.back_confusion: Spoofing works best for one-way attacks; a spoofed sender cannot complete a TCP handshake because the replies go elsewhere.
flashcards.back_hook: A fake return address on the envelope.

flashcards.back_definition: Sending huge numbers of fake MAC addresses to fill a switch's address table, so it starts sending frames out of every port and the attacker can sniff them.
flashcards.back_example: One laptop sends thousands of frames with random source MACs in a few seconds.
flashcards.back_confusion: Port security, which limits MAC addresses per port, stops it.
flashcards.back_hook: Overfill the switch's memory and it starts shouting.

flashcards.front: How does ARP spoofing put an attacker in the middle?
flashcards.back_definition: ARP has no authentication. The attacker sends forged ARP replies saying "the gateway's IP is at my MAC", so the victim's traffic flows through the attacker.
flashcards.back_example: The victim's ARP table suddenly shows the gateway with the attacker's MAC address.
flashcards.back_confusion: It needs only a spot on the same local network, not access to the router.
flashcards.back_hook: Lie about who lives at the address.

flashcards.back_definition: Dynamic ARP Inspection on switches, which checks ARP packets against a trusted table of IP-to-MAC bindings (built by DHCP snooping) and drops forgeries.
flashcards.back_example: A switch drops an ARP reply claiming the gateway IP from an access port.
flashcards.back_confusion: HTTPS protects the content of traffic, but it does not stop someone taking the middle position.
flashcards.back_hook: Check the claim against the register.

flashcards.back_definition: Getting a resolver to cache a fake name-to-IP answer, so everyone who uses that resolver is sent to the attacker's server.
flashcards.back_example: The attacker races the real answer with forged replies guessing the 16-bit transaction ID.
flashcards.back_confusion: It affects every user of the poisoned resolver, not just one person.
flashcards.back_hook: Poison the phone book, mislead the whole town.

flashcards.back_definition: It adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can check that an answer really came from the domain's owner and was not changed.
flashcards.back_example: A forged answer fails signature validation and is thrown away.
flashcards.back_confusion: DNSSEC proves the answer is genuine; it does not encrypt the lookup. DNS over HTTPS or TLS adds privacy.

flashcards.front: Promiscuous mode vs a SPAN port?
flashcards.back_definition: Promiscuous mode makes a network card accept every frame it receives. A SPAN (port mirror) makes a switch copy traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port.
flashcards.back_example: An IDS listens on a SPAN port to see all traffic to the server VLAN.
flashcards.back_confusion: On a switch, promiscuous mode alone sees little; the mirror or tap is what delivers the traffic.
flashcards.back_hook: Listen to everything vs have it copied to you.

flashcards.back_definition: A capture filter decides what gets recorded at all. A display filter hides already-captured packets you do not want to look at.
flashcards.back_confusion: A capture filter can't be undone; anything it excluded is gone.
flashcards.back_hook: Capture chooses what to keep; display chooses what to see.

flashcards.front: Which protocols send passwords in cleartext?
flashcards.back_definition: HTTP, Telnet, FTP and unencrypted POP3, IMAP and SMTP. Anyone who captures the traffic can read the login.
flashcards.back_example: A packet capture shows USER admin and PASS letmein on port 21.
flashcards.back_confusion: Use the encrypted versions: HTTPS, SSH, SFTP or FTPS, and mail over TLS.

flashcards.front: What made the 2016 Dyn attack so large?
flashcards.back_definition: The Mirai botnet of hijacked IoT devices, mostly cameras and routers with default passwords, flooded Dyn's DNS servers and made sites such as Twitter and Netflix unreachable for many users.
flashcards.back_example: Tens of thousands of webcams sent traffic at once.
flashcards.back_confusion: The websites themselves were fine; the DNS service that pointed people to them was down.
flashcards.back_hook: Knock out the signposts and nobody finds the town.

flashcards.back_definition: A worm using the EternalBlue exploit against SMBv1 (CVE-2017-0144) on unpatched Windows machines, encrypting files on each one.
flashcards.back_example: The UK's NHS cancelled thousands of appointments; Microsoft had released the patch (MS17-010) two months earlier.
flashcards.back_confusion: It needed no clicks: open SMB ports and missing patches were enough.
flashcards.back_hook: Patch, close port 445, or meet the worm.
